title: What he left
hookLine: no palace, no wealth, the Qur'an and his way
last: ALLAH IS ALIVE AND DOES NOT DIE.

cards: When a powerful person dies, there's usually an inventory. The houses, the accounts, the paintings, the lawyers arguing about who gets what.

By the end of his life, delegations had crossed Arabia to reach the Prophet ﷺ, bringing gifts. So what was in his estate? A companion named 'Amr ibn al-Harith answered that question, and al-Bukhari recorded it.
Aisha added a detail about his armor.

teach.h: A MULE, HIS WEAPONS, LAND GIVEN AWAY.
teach.b: 'Amr said: he left no gold coin and no silver coin, no servants, nothing, except his white mule, his weapons, and a piece of land he had given away as charity.

And Aisha said that when he died, his armor was held by a Jewish man in Medina, pawned as security for some barley. The man delegations crossed Arabia to meet died owing a neighbor for grain. But he did leave something.
A hadith says prophets don't leave gold or silver behind; they leave knowledge, and whoever takes it takes a great share. He left the Qur'an, and he left his way: the sunnah.
It means a way, a well-trodden path, an established custom. The sunnah is how he prayed, how he ate, how he treated his wives and children and animals, how he forgave, how he mended his own shoes.

The hadith are the reports that carry it; the sunnah is the way itself. Muslims hold to it alongside the Qur'an. A report in Sahih Muslim also speaks of the Book of God and his family, the ahl al-bayt.

Shia Muslims give that report special weight and receive the sunnah through the Prophet's family; Sunni Muslims, whose very name comes from sunnah, hold the family in honor too. And that closes this stretch of the path.

teach.h: FROM QUBA TO THE SMALL ROOM.
teach.b: Since Quba, you've walked through Medina with him: a mosque of palm trunks, brothers by choice, Badr and Uhud and the Trench, home life and the children and the animals, Hudaybiyyah and Mecca, the farewell, the small room.
No palace at the end. Just a way, trodden enough for others to walk.

how: Muslims follow the sunnah alongside the Qur'an, learning the Prophet's way through the hadith collections, in matters from prayer and fasting to eating, greeting and treating family and neighbors.

o: the Prophet's example, how he lived
the reports that record his sayings
the yearly fast in the month of Ramadan

games.q: what he left — tap the pairs.
p: the reports that carry the way

s: the Prophet ﷺ died a wealthy man
he left no gold or silver: a mule, his weapons, and land given as charity.
sunnah and hadith mean exactly the same thing
the hadith are the reports; the sunnah is the way they carry.
when he died, his armor was pawned for barley
Aisha said it was held by a Jewish man in Medina as security.

games.q: delegations arrive with gifts from across Arabia. your family needs barley. what do you do?
o: pawn your armor to a neighbor for it.
ask a delegation for more gifts.
games.why: Aisha said his armor was pawned to a Jewish man in Medina for barley, still pawned when he died.

practice: Picture the room you live in and everything in it, and pick one thing you don't need that has some worth, a coat, a book, a tool, some money, and decide who it will go to.
Hold that decision, and notice whether your hand wants to close around it. If you pray, you can ask that what you leave behind be a way and not a pile.

wordCard.voice: Sunnah. The Prophet's way, a well-trodden path, carried in the hadith and followed alongside the Qur'an. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a way, a custom, a well-trodden path. the Prophet's way, followed alongside the Qur'an.

carryVoice: Your line: he left the way. A mule, his weapons, pawned armor, and a path to walk. See you tomorrow.
